learn.hook: The Himalaya are still rising, yet the Ganga carries away millions of tonnes of their rock every year. The earth's surface is a tug-of-war between building up and wearing down.
points: Endogenic forces (internal) build up or elevate parts of the earth's surface; exogenic forces (external) wear down relief (degradation) and fill up basins (aggradation). Wearing down of relief through erosion is called gradation.

Geomorphic processes are the endogenic and exogenic forces that cause physical stresses and chemical actions on earth materials and change the configuration of the earth's surface. Diastrophism and volcanism are endogenic; weathering, mass wasting, erosion and deposition are exogenic.
A geomorphic agent is a mobile medium that removes, transports and deposits earth materials: running water, groundwater, glaciers, wind, waves and currents.
Gravity is a directional force that activates all downslope movements of matter and also causes stresses on earth materials. All movements occur due to gradients, from higher to lower levels.

example.q: Classify as endogenic or exogenic: (a) uplift of a plateau; (b) a river carrying sand to the sea; (c) a volcanic eruption; (d) breaking of rock by frost.
steps: Endogenic processes come from inside the earth: uplift (a) and volcanism (c).
Exogenic processes act on the surface using external energy: river transport (b) and frost weathering (d).

learn.reallife: The Brahmaputra deposits huge amounts of sediment in Assam's valley (aggradation), while the Himalaya it drains are lifted by endogenic forces.

learn.hook: The heat that lifts the Himalaya comes from deep inside the earth: radioactive elements and heat left over from the planet's birth.
points: The energy from within the earth drives endogenic processes. It is mostly generated by radioactivity, rotational and tidal friction, and primordial heat from the origin of the earth. Through geothermal gradients and heat flow, it induces diastrophism and volcanism.
Diastrophism: all processes that move, elevate or build up portions of the earth's crust.
Orogeny (orogenic processes): mountain building through severe folding, affecting long and narrow belts of the crust.
Epeirogeny (epeirogenic processes): uplift or warping of large parts of the crust. It causes simple deformation; it is a continent-building process, while orogeny is mountain building.

Diastrophism also includes earthquakes (local, relatively minor movements) and plate tectonics (horizontal movements of crustal plates). Diastrophism produces faulting and fracturing, and changes in pressure, volume and temperature that can cause metamorphism.

example.q: Distinguish orogeny and epeirogeny with one feature each.
steps: Orogeny: severe folding in long, narrow belts → mountains (e.g. Himalaya).
Epeirogeny: uplift or warping of large parts of the crust with simple deformation → continent building.
So the key difference is severe folding of narrow belts vs broad uplift of large areas.
example.answer: Orogeny = mountain building by severe folding of narrow belts; epeirogeny = broad uplift/warping of large areas (continent building).

learn.reallife: Hot springs at Manikaran in Himachal Pradesh and Bakreshwar in West Bengal are surface signs of the earth's internal heat.

learn.hook: Push on a stack of books from the side and the top ones slide. Rocks feel the same 'shear', and that is how they start to break.
points: Volcanism (an endogenic process) includes the movement of molten rock (magma) onto or towards the earth's surface, and the formation of intrusive and extrusive volcanic forms.
Exogenic processes get their energy from the atmosphere, determined ultimately by the sun, and from the gradients created by tectonic factors.

Stress is force applied per unit area. It is produced in a solid by pushing or pulling and causes deformation. Forces acting along the faces of earth materials are shear stresses (separating forces); they break rocks and cause angular displacement or slippage.

Earth materials also face molecular stresses from temperature changes, crystallisation and melting. Chemical processes loosen bonds between grains. When stress exceeds a material's resistance, it breaks.
Weathering, mass wasting/movements, erosion and transportation are together called denudation, which means to strip off or uncover.

steps: Stress = force ÷ area.
= 200 newtons per m².

learn.hook: The same granite crumbles in a different way in Rajasthan's heat, Kerala's rain and Ladakh's frost. Climate decides which exogenic processes rule.
points: Exogenic processes depend on the type of climate. Temperature and precipitation are the two most important climatic elements controlling them.
Vegetation density and type, which depend on precipitation and temperature, also influence exogenic processes indirectly.

Within a climatic region, there are local variations due to altitude, aspect (north- vs south-facing slopes receiving different insolation), wind speed and direction, rainfall intensity, and freeze-thaw cycles.
Rock type and structure matter too: differences in rocks lead to differential erosion, so soft rocks wear away faster than hard ones.
NCERT's diagram shows denudational processes (weathering, mass wasting, erosion and transportation) together with the driving forces behind them, such as solar energy, gravity and gradients.

example.q: Two slopes of the same hill in the mid-latitudes of the Northern Hemisphere face north and south. Why might exogenic processes differ on them?
steps: The south-facing slope receives more sunlight (insolation).
It is warmer and drier; the north-facing slope is cooler and moister.
Different temperature and moisture lead to different weathering and vegetation.
So aspect causes local differences in exogenic processes.
example.answer: Because of aspect: the sunnier south-facing slope is warmer and drier than the cooler, moister north-facing slope.

learn.reallife: In the Kumaon Himalaya, villages and orchards prefer the sunny south-facing slopes, while north-facing slopes keep denser, moister forests.

learn.hook: Without weathering there would be no soil, no forests and no bauxite for aluminium. Slow-motion rock breaking is the foundation of life and industry.
points: Weathering is the mechanical disintegration and chemical decomposition of rocks through the actions of the elements of weather and climate.
Very little or no motion of material takes place in weathering, so it is an in-situ or on-site process.
Weathering is controlled by many geological, climatic, topographic and vegetative factors. Weathering processes are grouped as chemical, physical (mechanical) and biological.

Significance: weathering breaks rocks into smaller fragments, preparing the way for regolith and soils, and for erosion and mass movements. Forests and biodiversity depend on the depth of the weathering mantle.

Weathering helps in the enrichment and concentration of valuable ores of iron, manganese, aluminium and copper. When some materials are leached away, the concentration of the remaining valuable material rises, making it economic to mine. This is called enrichment.

example.q: A rock contains 20 kg of aluminium ore mixed in 100 kg of material. Weathering leaches away 50 kg of other material. What is the new percentage of ore?
steps: Original ore share = 20 ÷ 100 = 20%.
After leaching, total = 100 − 50 = 50 kg; ore is still 20 kg.
Ore concentration has doubled: enrichment.
example.answer: 40%, the ore has been enriched by weathering.

learn.reallife: India's bauxite deposits in Odisha and Jharkhand, the source of aluminium, formed by intense weathering that removed other minerals and concentrated aluminium.

learn.hook: Rainwater is slightly acidic. Given enough time, it can dissolve whole caves out of limestone.
points: Chemical weathering processes include solution, carbonation, hydration, oxidation and reduction. They act on rocks to decompose, dissolve or reduce them to fine particles, with water and air and heat speeding them up.

Solution: minerals dissolve in water or acids. Nitrates, sulphates and potassium are very soluble; common salt (sodium chloride) also dissolves. Calcium carbonate and calcium magnesium bicarbonate in limestones dissolve in water containing carbonic acid.

Carbonation: the reaction of carbonate and bicarbonate with minerals. Carbon dioxide from the air and soil air dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, a weak acid, which dissolves calcium and magnesium carbonates. This helps form caves.

Hydration: chemical addition of water. Minerals take up water and expand, increasing volume. Calcium sulphate takes in water and turns into gypsum, which is more unstable. Repeated hydration causes fatigue in rocks and may lead to disintegration.

Oxidation: combination of a mineral with oxygen to form oxides or hydroxides, where air and oxygenated water are available; iron, manganese and sulphur are commonly involved (rusting of iron is an example). Reduction occurs when oxidised minerals are placed where oxygen is absent, e.g. below the water table or in waterlogged ground.

steps: (a) CO₂ + water → carbonic acid, which dissolves carbonates → carbonation.
(b) Addition of water to a mineral → hydration.
(c) Combination with oxygen → oxidation.

topics.title: Physical weathering: unloading, temperature and exfoliation

learn.hook: The smooth, rounded granite domes and boulders of the Deccan look polished, but no one polished them. The rock peeled itself like an onion.
points: Physical (mechanical) weathering depends on applied forces: gravitational forces (overburden pressure, load, shearing stress); expansion forces due to temperature changes, crystal growth or animal activity; and water pressure controlled by wetting and drying cycles.

Unloading and expansion: continued erosion removes the overlying rock load, releasing vertical pressure. The upper layers expand, and fractures develop roughly parallel to the surface. On curved surfaces this produces exfoliation sheets and large, smooth rounded exfoliation domes.

Temperature changes and expansion: surface layers expand more than deeper rock, creating stress that causes heaving and fracturing parallel to the surface. Differential heating and cooling leads to exfoliation and smooth rounded surfaces; in granites, rounded boulders called tors form.
Exfoliation is a result, not a process: it is the flaking off of curved sheets of rock. Exfoliation domes result from unloading, and tors from thermal expansion.

example.q: A granite hill has become a huge smooth dome after the overlying rocks were eroded away. Explain the weathering involved.
steps: Erosion removed the overlying load from the granite.
Pressure release allowed the upper granite layers to expand.
Fractures developed parallel to the curved surface.
Curved sheets peeled off (exfoliation), producing a smooth exfoliation dome.
example.answer: Unloading and expansion produced exfoliation, forming an exfoliation dome.

learn.hook: Water expands when it freezes, salt crystals grow in desert rocks, and tree roots push like hydraulic jacks. Small forces, repeated endlessly, crack mountains.
points: Frost weathering occurs due to the growth of ice in pores and cracks during repeated cycles of freezing and melting. It is most effective at high elevations in mid-latitudes, where freezing and thawing are repeated often; glacial areas face frost wedging daily. Rapid freezing causes sudden expansion and high pressure.

Salt weathering: salts in rocks expand due to thermal action, hydration and crystallisation. Salts of calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and barium tend to expand. High surface temperatures of 30–50°C in deserts favour salt expansion.

Salt crystals in near-surface pores split grains, which fall off: granular disintegration or granular foliation. Salt crystallisation is the most effective salt-weathering process, favoured by alternate wetting and drying.

Biological weathering: burrowing and wedging by earthworms, termites and rodents expose new surfaces to chemical attack; humans disturb vegetation and plough soils. Decaying plant and animal matter produces humic, carbonic and other acids. Plant roots exert tremendous pressure and break rocks apart.

example.q: Match each place to its most effective weathering: (a) high-altitude slopes of Himachal with daily freeze-thaw; (b) the hot, dry Thar desert with salty soils; (c) a forest where tree roots grow into rock cracks.
steps: (a) Repeated freezing and thawing → frost wedging.
(b) High temperatures and salts → salt weathering (salt crystallisation).
(c) Roots growing in cracks → biological weathering.
example.answer: (a) Frost wedging; (b) Salt weathering; (c) Biological weathering.

topics.title: Mass movements: causes, forms and slow movements

learn.hook: Ever seen electric poles on a hillside all leaning downhill? The soil beneath them is creeping, too slowly to see.
points: Mass movements transfer rock debris down slopes under the direct influence of gravity. Air, water or ice do not carry the debris; rather, the debris may carry air, water or ice with it. Mass movements do not come under erosion.

Factors favouring them: weak unconsolidated materials, thinly bedded rocks, faults, steep slopes, heavy rainfall and scarce vegetation. Activating causes include removal of support from below, increase in gradient and height of slopes, overloading (by materials or heavy rain and saturation), earthquakes, explosions or machinery, excessive seepage, drawdown of water from reservoirs, and removal of natural vegetation.
Three forms of movement: heave (heaving up of soils due to frost growth and other causes), flow and slide.

Slow movements: creep occurs on moderately steep, soil-covered slopes and is extremely slow and imperceptible; leaning fence posts and poles show soil creep. Types include soil creep, talus creep, rock creep and rock-glacier creep.

Solifluction is the slow downslope flow of soil or fine debris saturated or lubricated with water. It is common in moist temperate areas, where surface melting of deeply frozen ground and long continued rain occur.

example.q: After road widening on a Himalayan hill, the toe of a slope is cut away and heavy monsoon rain follows. Which activating causes of mass movement are present?
steps: Cutting the toe removes support from below.
It also steepens the slope (increase in gradient).
Heavy rain saturates and overloads slope materials.
Together these make mass movement likely.
example.answer: Removal of support, increased gradient, and overloading/saturation by heavy rain.

learn.hook: In the Himalaya, a single night of cloudburst can send a hillside crashing onto a highway. Why do the Himalaya suffer more than the Western Ghats?
points: Rapid movements are common in humid regions on gentle to steep slopes. Earthflow: water-saturated clayey or silty material moves down low-angle terraces or hillsides, often slumping into step-like terraces.

Mudflow: with heavy rain and no vegetation, thick weathered layers saturated with water flow down definite channels like streams of mud. They can engulf roads, bridges and houses, and occur often on slopes of erupting or recently erupted volcanoes. Debris avalanche: on steep slopes in narrow tracks, even faster than mudflow, similar to a snow avalanche.

Landslides are relatively rapid and perceptible movements of relatively dry material. Types: slump (slipping with a backward rotation), debris slide (rolling or sliding without backward rotation), debris fall (nearly free fall from a vertical face), rock slide (sliding of rock masses down bedding, joint or fault surfaces) and rock fall (free fall of rock blocks from a steep slope).
Debris avalanches and landslides are very frequent in the Himalaya because they are tectonically active, made mostly of sedimentary rocks and unconsolidated deposits, and have very steep slopes.

The Nilgiris and Western Ghats are tectonically stable and made of hard rocks, yet landslides occur there because of very steep slopes and cliffs, strong mechanical weathering due to temperature changes, and heavy rainfall over short periods.

example.answer: Slump (with backward rotation); a debris slide has no backward rotation.

learn.hook: Weathering is a rock breaking at home. Erosion is the rock leaving home, on a river, a glacier or a gust of wind.
points: Erosion involves the acquisition and transportation of rock debris. It is largely responsible for the continuous changes in the earth's surface.
Weathering is in-situ and involves no motion; erosion involves movement of material. Weathering aids erosion, but it is not a pre-condition for erosion.

Erosion and transportation are controlled by kinetic energy. The agents are running water, wind, glaciers, waves and groundwater; the first three are controlled by climate. Abrasion by debris carried by agents greatly aids erosion.

Running water is the most important agent in humid regions with heavy rainfall; wind operates mainly in hot dry deserts; glaciers work in high latitudes and high altitudes; waves act along coasts; groundwater is effective in limestone areas.

Deposition is a consequence of erosion: when agents lose velocity and energy on gentler slopes, they drop their load. Coarser materials are deposited first and finer ones later. Deposition is not the work of a separate agent.

example.q: A river slows down as it enters the plains from the hills. What happens to its load and in what order?
steps: Velocity drops on the gentler slope, so energy falls.
The river can no longer carry all its load and starts depositing.
Coarse material (boulders, gravel) settles first.
Finer material (sand, silt, clay) is carried farther and settles later.
example.answer: It deposits its load: coarse material first, finer material later.

topics.title: Soil formation: process, profile, parent material and topography

learn.hook: A handful of good soil can take centuries to form, and it starts with bacteria, lichens and mosses settling on broken rock.
points: Soil is a collection of natural bodies on the earth's surface containing living matter and supporting or capable of supporting plants. It is a dynamic medium with constant chemical, physical and biological activity.

Soil formation (pedogenesis) depends first on weathering; the weathering mantle is the basic input. Weathered material or transported deposits are colonised by bacteria and simple plants like mosses and lichens; dead remains build humus; grasses, ferns, bushes and trees follow. Roots and burrowing animals make it porous; a mature soil, a mix of mineral and organic products, forms and develops layers (horizons) seen in a soil profile.
Five soil-forming factors: parent material, topography, climate, biological activity and time. They act together.

Parent material is a passive control factor. It can be in-situ weathered rock debris (residual soils) or transported deposits (transported soils). Texture, structure and mineral composition of the debris matter.

Topography is another passive factor: soils are thin on steep slopes and thick on flat uplands; gentle slopes with slow erosion and good percolation favour soil formation. In middle latitudes, sunny south-facing slopes and cool, moist north-facing slopes develop different soils and vegetation.

example.q: Why is soil usually thin on a steep hillside but thick on a flat upland?
steps: On steep slopes, erosion removes weathered material quickly.
Water runs off instead of percolating, so less weathering at depth.
On flat uplands, material stays in place and water percolates well.
So soil accumulates and becomes thick.
example.answer: Steep slopes lose material to erosion; flat uplands retain it, so soil is thicker there.

learn.reallife: Alluvial soils of the Ganga plain are transported soils, while the black soils of the Deccan formed in place from basalt: residual soils.

topics.title: Soil formation: climate, biological activity and time

learn.hook: The same parent rock can give a deep red soil in Kerala and a thin, stony soil in Ladakh. Climate, life and time make the difference.
points: Climate is an important active factor: moisture (intensity, frequency and duration of precipitation; evaporation; humidity) and temperature (seasonal and daily variation).

Excess water moves soil components downward (eluviation) and deposits them below (illuviation). In wet equatorial areas, calcium, sodium, magnesium, potassium and much of the silica are removed; removal of silica is desilication. In dry climates, evaporation exceeds precipitation, groundwater rises by capillary action and leaves salts that form a crust called hardpan. In tropical areas with intermediate rainfall, calcium carbonate nodules (kanker) form.
Higher temperature increases chemical activity (except carbonation), so tropical soils have deeper profiles; in frozen tundra, soils are mainly mechanically broken material.

Biological activity: vegetation and organisms add organic matter, moisture retention and nitrogen. Dead plants give humus. In cold climates, slow bacterial activity lets humus and peat accumulate; in humid tropics, intense bacterial action leaves low humus. Nitrogen fixation: Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants fix nitrogen. Earthworms, ants, termites and rodents rework the soil.

Time: the length of time soil-forming processes operate determines maturity and profile development. Soils on recent alluvium or glacial till are young, with no or poorly developed horizons. No fixed absolute time can be set for soils to mature.

example.q: Why do humid tropical soils have low humus even though plant growth is heavy?
steps: Humid tropics are hot and wet.
Bacterial growth and action are intense there.
Dead vegetation is rapidly oxidised (decomposed).
So little humus accumulates in the soil.
example.answer: Intense bacterial activity rapidly decomposes dead matter, leaving little humus.
